name: Floci
license: MIT (all four emulators, the CLI and the Testcontainers modules)
summary: A young, MIT-licensed family of local emulators for AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud, built as a free drop-in for LocalStack and pitched at AI coding agents.
intro: Floci is four separate emulators, each a single Docker image with one port: `floci` for AWS on 4566, `floci-az` for Azure on 4577, `floci-gcp` for Google Cloud on 4588 and `floci-oci` for Oracle Cloud on 4599. They are written in Java on Quarkus and compiled ahead of time to native binaries with GraalVM Mandrel, so the project measures a start in about 24 ms and about 13 MiB of memory at idle. Simple services such as S3, SQS, SNS, DynamoDB, IAM and Step Functions are emulated inside the process, with state kept in memory or, if you choose, flushed to disk or a write-ahead log. Where that would be too shallow, Floci starts real engines through the Docker socket: Lambda functions in AWS’s runtime images, RDS as real PostgreSQL, MySQL or MariaDB, ElastiCache as Valkey, MSK as Redpanda and EKS as k3s. Any credentials work; IAM and service control policies are evaluated only if you turn enforcement on.

The AWS emulator is built to replace LocalStack’s retired Community image. It answers on the same port, translates LocalStack’s environment variables, runs scripts from `/etc/localstack/init/`, serves `/_localstack/health` and prints the `Ready.` line that Testcontainers waits for, so moving is usually a one-line image change. It is free for any use: no account, no auth token, no paid tiers and no telemetry. The website now leads with AI coding agents: point the agent at Floci instead of a real account, so there are no cloud credentials to leak and nothing to bill. The project is seven months old and moves fast, with releases every two weeks.
strengths: MIT licence with no account, token, feature gates or telemetry, so it can run in any company’s CI or be embedded in other tools
Drop-in for LocalStack Community setups: same port, translated settings, init scripts and health endpoint
Small and fast by its own benchmarks: a native binary that starts in milliseconds, in an image of about 80 MB compressed (September 2026)
Broad AWS coverage (about 125 services by its own count), with real Docker-backed engines for Lambda, RDS, ElastiCache, MSK and EKS
One model across four clouds, plus Testcontainers modules for Java, Go, Node.js, Python and .NET
limits: Young: first commit in March 2026, releases every two weeks, and a 2.0 in September that already broke some Step Functions definitions
Coverage counts are self-reported and uneven: Bedrock Runtime returns canned answers, Textract and Transcribe return dummy data, and FIS experiments inject no faults
The Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud emulators are pre-1.0, and the creator says they are short of maintainers; `floci-gcp` has no second maintainer
No company or paid support behind it; the project leans on one lead maintainer and volunteers
Docker-backed services need the host’s Docker socket, and the documented setup runs the container as root, which hands it control of the host’s Docker

source: image: floci/floci:latest   # MIT, no account or token
- /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock  # Lambda, RDS, ElastiCache run as real containers
FLOCI_STORAGE_MODE: memory                      # a clean cloud on every start
FLOCI_SERVICES_IAM_ENFORCEMENT_ENABLED: "true"  # check IAM policies (off by default)

sections.title: Floci and LocalStack
sections.intro: Floci exists because of LocalStack’s 2026 change, so this is the comparison most readers need.

story: In December 2025 LocalStack announced that its free, open-source Community image would stop getting updates and that, from March 2026, current releases would need an account and an auth token, even in CI. Hector Ventura, a developer in Texas, pushed the first commit of Floci on 15 March 2026 and tagged 1.0.0 the same day: an MIT-licensed AWS emulator on LocalStack’s port, first published as `hectorvent/floci`. The name comes from floccus, a cloud formation that looks like popcorn.

The timing found an audience. A month in, Ventura counted nearly 4,000 GitHub stars, more than 60 contributors and over 450 merged pull requests. The project moved to the `floci-io` organisation and added emulators for Azure in April, Google Cloud in May and Oracle Cloud in July. By mid-September it had shipped 2.0, passed 24,000 stars and 2.6 million Docker pulls, and counted 284 contributors on the AWS emulator, among them, he notes, Maven’s creator Jason van Zyl and David Phillips, a creator of Presto and Trino.
Ventura’s monthly reports are candid about the weak spots: outside AWS the emulators lack maintainers, and in one recent month he wrote 73% of what merged on the Oracle Cloud emulator himself.

choices.why: Ventura’s stated goal is for Floci to be the smallest, fastest thing in a pipeline. Compiling Java ahead of time with GraalVM Mandrel removes JVM warm-up, so the emulator can start inside an edit loop or a small CI runner.
Most users arrive from LocalStack, so Floci keeps port 4566, translates `LOCALSTACK_*` settings, runs the same init scripts and prints the same readiness line. Switching becomes a one-line change.

choices.choice: Real containers where emulation would be shallow
choices.why: Databases, brokers and function runtimes are hard to fake well, so Floci starts real PostgreSQL, Valkey, Redpanda, k3s and AWS Lambda runtime images instead of imitating them.

choices.choice: MIT, with no gates and no telemetry
choices.why: A direct answer to the Community sunset: every service for every user, nothing to sign up for, and nothing to stop a company from forking or embedding it.

timeline.text: LocalStack announces the end of its free Community image (December)
First commit and 1.0.0 on 15 March, a week before LocalStack’s switch
Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud emulators arrive between April and July
